The mouth opens underneath the head. Inside are overlapping mineral-hardened plates, more like a rasp than teeth. It scrapes microbial growth from warm rock and grinds the small, armored grazers living among it.

It has no eyes, not even buried remnants of them.

Instead, a fringe of filaments surrounds its head. Some taste the water for dissolved chemicals. Others register warmth. The longest detect currents so faint that a small swimmer passing several body lengths away leaves a readable disturbance.

The hushback’s most sensitive organs are in its feet.

Standing still, it feels the seabed.

A shifting stone, a digging animal, the pulse of water through a vent—all reach it as vibrations. It can distinguish the irregular scraping of prey from the slow fracture of unstable rock.
